Article Title: 10-year-old Seattle boy lived in a tent while his mother battled fentanyl addiction; after an 11-month rescue effort, he entered school for the first time and said, 'I want to go back'
Article Text:
The boy had been living in difficult conditions and had never experienced school before. (Representational photo. Credit: The Seattle Times)

Neighbours kept raising concerns

The boy had been living in the tent with his mother, who was struggling with fentanyl addiction

A fresh new start

Many families still need help

Bullying/stigmatization Academic challenges Emotional trauma Adjustment to a new environment 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A 10-year-old boy in Seattle walked into a school for the first time last week after spending much of his childhood living in a tent in a North Seattle park. His first day of school came after an 11-month effort by a local nonprofit, neighbours and others to help him and his mother move out of life on the streets.The boy had been living in the tent with his mother, who was struggling with fentanyl addiction and was being sexually exploited, according to Kristine Moreland, executive director of The More We Love, a Kirkland-based organisation that works with homeless women and children, KRI reported. The boy's father had also refused offers of housing, food and other services.Moreland said the boy had been living in difficult conditions and had never experienced school before. “This young man has been in fight or flight since the day he was born,” she said. After his first day in the classroom, however, the boy gave the people who had been helping him a simple response. “I want to go back.”His journey towards school began in October last year, when Moreland and her team first visited the tent where the boy was living. At the time, he was alone in the tent. The situation had already drawn the attention of neighbours, who had repeatedly contacted the Seattle Police Department and Child Protective Services.According to Moreland, authorities had determined on several occasions that the boy was not in imminent danger. The nonprofit, however, continued visiting the tent and trying to help the family.“Everybody kept saying the same thing: He is ok. He is safe,” Moreland said. “We continued to show up at that tent, knowing that that was not the case.”The situation received wider attention in December after KIRO Newsradio reported on the boy. Moreland was recorded offering the family immediate shelter, including a private room that was available that day. The boy's father rejected the offer. “Not from you,” he told her.The situation changed in the early hours of New Year's Day. A Seattle police officer called Moreland and told her that the boy and his mother were ready to accept help. The mother entered treatment for active fentanyl addiction, while The More We Love helped connect her with recovery services.The organisation also arranged behavioural health treatment for the boy through Seattle Children's Hospital. Moreland said her team worked with another mission to find long-term housing for the family. However, that agency was unable to manage the boy's behavioural challenges and the family was released back to the streets.That did not end the effort to help them. “We said, not a chance. Our case managers have dug in day after day, helping this little man get through this,” Moreland said.The boy's mother remains in recovery, Moreland said. She described that progress as a big deal while also pointing to the difficulties involved in learning to parent while dealing with addiction and trauma.“She has been in the cycle predominantly her whole life,” Moreland said. “We really have to work on her traumas as well.”For the boy, the nonprofit's work did not stop with getting him into school. Moreland said the boy still faces challenges as he adjusts to a new life, including the possibility of being bullied at school. She said people should not romanticise what comes next simply because he has now reached a classroom.“And what if he was still living in the tent?” Moreland said. “Then where would he be?”Moreland said the boy's situation is not unique. She said she receives calls every day from law enforcement and community partners about women and children living in encampments across the region.The More We Love has also received a $500,000 matching donation from an anonymous donor to support efforts to help women and children living in encampments. Moreland said donations to the organisation through its website would be matched.The privately funded nonprofit also operates a crisis centre where staff care for infants born exposed to fentanyl. Moreland said the organisation needs volunteers to help comfort and care for the babies.Moreland has worked in outreach in Seattle for nearly 25 years. She said the 10-year-old now has “an army of encouragement behind him” as he begins school and adjusts to a different life. “This is hope to me,” she said. “And reminds me to continue every single day in this work.”
Article Summary: 10-year-old boy walked into a school for the first time last week after spending much of his childhood living in a tent in a North Seattle park. His first day of school came after an 11-month effort by a local nonprofit, neighbours and others to help him and his mother move out of life on the streets. The boy had been living in the tent with his mother, who was struggling with fentanyl addiction.

Article Title: A Tennessee farmer spent 4 years trying to return a mistaken $20,000 IRS refund. Instead, he faced $4,000 in penalties; then country singer John Rich stepped in and ended the dispute
Article Text:
The government’s mistake came at his expense

Pic credit: WTVF

His battle made it to the news

Resolving the problem that was never his to begin with

After a four-year battle with the IRS, Wilson Perry Kirby, a Middle Tennessee farmer, finally got an acknowledgement that the government had indeed made a mistake. In 2022, Kirby received a $20,000 tax refund he knew wasn't meant for him. Instead of cashing it, he immediately tried to return the money. But instead, the IRS responded by charging him $4,000 in interest and withholding his own $1,800 refund, according to a report by WTVF. When the incident got media coverage, country music star John Rich saw the report and tried to untangle what four years of official channels couldn't fix. This month, Kirby finally received his refund, along with two apology letters from the agencies involved.All of Kirby’s trouble started in 2022, when the IRS sent him a $20,000 tax refund. Wilson Perry Kirby, a retired Montgomery County Highway Department worker and farmer from Coopertown, Tennessee, knew the money didn’t belong to him. So he contacted his accountant and filed the paperwork. They waited for the agency to acknowledge the error and process the return. That's where everything stalled.Instead of acknowledging the mistake and accepting the money back, the IRS charged him $4,000 in interest for holding on to it.Kirby was speechless: he hadn’t spent a penny, and in fact, all he did was try to return it. But the agency treated him like a debtor. To make it worse, the IRS withheld his own $1,800 tax refund to put towards the interest he supposedly owed.At this point, the Tennessee farmer was helpless. He reached out to anyone who might help, including government officials, his state senator's office, county representatives, the mayor, the governor and even the president's office. But none of his appeals were answered. A farmer trying to do the right thing got bureaucratic silence in return.This process dragged on for years and the stress mounted. He saw no resolution. It was absurd: a debt he didn’t owe was growing, while the IRS held back his $1,800 refund. The financial pressure and emotional toll broke him.Making things worse, Kirby lost his wife, Norma Jean, in August 2024. She was the one managing every aspect of his life, including the paperwork related to this trouble. Suddenly, he was all alone, both in life and in dealing with a problem he had been trying to resolve for years. He didn’t know how to navigate this federal nightmare alone. He was just an elderly farmer lost in grief, running the farm and fighting a battle against an agency that wouldn't acknowledge its own mistake. And for that, he was about to lose his own farm. An IRS notice reportedly warned Kirby that if he did not pay the interest it said he owed, he risked having his property seized.With no options left, Kirby turned to the media, hoping they could help him fight his battle. This spring, a reporter from WTVF brought the Tennessee farmer’s ordeal to light, detailing his four-year struggle with the IRS and the financial and emotional toll it had taken on him.The coverage caught the attention of John Rich, the country music artist appointed as Special Envoy for American Landowners. Rich, who was in Italy, saw the coverage and decided to step in, leveraging his position to untangle what four years of official channels couldn't. “Well, Mr. Kirby is a landowner, and his land is under threat, and he didn’t do anything wrong, and he is at his wits’ end with this thing, and I want to see what I can do,” Rich told the broadcaster.In a video shared on X in July this year, Rich assured viewers that Mr Kirby’s land wouldn’t be at risk and that the whole issue would soon be resolved. “Nobody is taking Mr Kirby’s farm. This is about to get HANDLED,” the singer said. Following this, in September, he met Kirby and assured him that the issue would be dealt with.What Kirby has been waiting years to see has finally arrived. Earlier this month, he finally received his $1,800 refund that the IRS had withheld. The money surely mattered. But what mattered more was what came with it. John Rich drove out to Kirby's farm with two apology letters. Two formal acknowledgements from the agencies involved. They acknowledged the mistake. Kirby was right all along. “He says he almost took his own life over the thought of losing his farm, but we managed to save it,” Rich said in a post shared on X. “Big thanks to @SecRollins who fights like a Titan for our farmers every day, and is a true Patriot🇺🇸 ‘Love Thy Neighbor As Thyself’.”After four years, a grandfather and farmer finally got what he should have gotten in 2022: an acknowledgement of the truth. Kirby is relieved that the nightmare is finally over.
Article Summary: Tennessee farmer Wilson Perry Kirby received a $20,000 tax refund in 2022. He immediately tried to return the money, but the IRS wouldn't acknowledge the mistake. Instead, the IRS charged him $4,000 in interest for holding on to the money. The IRS also withheld his own $1,800 tax refund to put towards the interest he supposedly owed. Country music star John Rich saw the story and decided to help Kirby resolve the issue.

Article Title: In 1967, Rolex made a rare yellow-gold Daytona with a Paul Newman dial; after more than 45 years in a family drawer, two sisters inherited it and it sold for CHF 1.143 million in Geneva
Article Text:
The watch had been left forgotten in a drawer for more than 45 years. (Representational AI photo)

A rare yellow-gold Daytona

Its final price was much higher than the auction house’s estimate.

Why the Reference 6239 is important

Only about 300 yellow-gold examples

A rare Rolex Daytona made in 1967 and kept in a family drawer for more than 45 years sold for CHF 1.143 million at auction in Geneva. The 18k yellow-gold watch, a Reference 6239 with a black and champagne “Paul Newman” dial, belonged to the family of its original owner. It was later inherited by two sisters before being offered at auction.According to Phillips Auction, the watch was listed by Sotheby’s with an estimate of CHF 300,000 to CHF 600,000. Its final price was much higher than the auction house’s estimate. The sale drew attention to the rarity of yellow-gold versions of the early Rolex Daytona, particularly those fitted with the Paul Newman-style dial.The Reference 6239 has an important place in the history of the Daytona. Rolex launched the model in 1963, and it was discontinued only a few years later. Sotheby’s estimates that around 14,000 examples of the Reference 6239 were produced, with only about 300 made in yellow gold.That already makes the yellow-gold version a small part of the total production. The watch sold in Geneva is rarer still because of its Paul Newman dial. Sotheby’s research suggests that only about 10 gold Reference 6239 watches with Paul Newman dials have resurfaced on the market.The watch has an 18k yellow-gold case measuring 37 mm in diameter. It has a black dial with champagne-coloured registers and is powered by Rolex calibre 722-1, a manually wound movement with 17 jewels. The case, dial and movement are all signed.Its case number is 1’757’928. The watch has a gold-plated Rolex buckle and a screw-down case back. It does not come with its original box, papers or other accessories.Sotheby’s said the watch came directly from the family of the original owner. It had been left forgotten in a drawer for more than 45 years. That history was an important part of the watch’s provenance when it was presented for sale. The watch was also described as being in exceptional condition.The Reference 6239 was the first Daytona model produced by Rolex, according to Sotheby’s. The model was launched in 1963 and was created for the world of endurance racing. Its design combined a mechanical chronograph with a tachymeter scale, features associated with its racing purpose.The few yellow-gold examples have details that set them apart from the more common steel watches. Sotheby’s described the gold versions as having refined dial details, champagne tones, gilt markers and distinctive graphics.The Paul Newman dial is another feature that makes these watches particularly sought after by collectors. The term refers to a specific dial layout used on some vintage Daytona models. The yellow-gold watch sold by Sotheby’s has a black dial with champagne registers.Another yellow-gold Reference 6239, known as “The Golden Pagoda”, was also highlighted by Phillips in its coverage of a 2025 Geneva auction. Phillips described that watch as having a champagne “Paul Newman” dial and said it was one of the rarest versions of the Daytona.Phillips said that around 14,000 Reference 6239 Daytonas were produced between 1963 and 1969, while only about 300 were made in yellow gold. This means the gold version was a very small part of the total production.The yellow-gold watches also differed from the steel versions in their appearance. Phillips described the champagne Paul Newman dial as having a warm finish, with three recessed registers and gold graphics.The auction house also noted that gold was not the usual choice for a Daytona at the time. The Cosmograph was designed as a functional chronograph, while Rolex’s gold watches were more commonly associated with dressier models.Over time, however, rare examples of the Daytona became important pieces for collectors. Condition, originality and provenance can be particularly significant when vintage watches are offered at auction.
Article Summary: The 18k yellow-gold watch, a Reference 6239 with a black and champagne “Paul Newman’ dial, belonged to the family of its original owner. It was later inherited by two sisters before being offered at auction. Sotheby’s estimates that around 14,000 examples were produced, with only about 300 made in yellow gold.

Article Title: An 82-year-old California tea importer spent 53 years on a 2-acre compound with 36+ structures; after decades of permit disputes and a 2024 National Register listing, a court ordered him to leave
Article Text:
Hoffman has acknowledged that the buildings lacked proper permits but has maintained that they were not unsafe. Enforcement actions and fines did little to prevent continued activity at the property.

For more than half a century, two acres in the hills of Lagunitas became the home, workplace and personal vision of California tea importer David Lee Hoffman. Over the decades, the property evolved into a maze of handmade buildings, caves and other structures, earning the name The Last Resort. Now, after years of legal battles over permits and code enforcement, Hoffman has been forced to leave, reports SFGATE. Scroll down to read his journey of struggle.A decades-long building battleAccording to SFGATE, Hoffman, 82, moved onto the Marin County property more than 53 years ago. Beginning in the 1970s and 1980s, he constructed structures that supported his approach to sustainable living and provided storage for his tea business and other belongings. The compound eventually grew to at least 36 structures, many of them built without the permits required by the county. A neighbor's tip brought the property to the county's attention. Officials issued the first stop-work order in 1988, beginning a long-running dispute over whether the structures should be removed, legalized or preserved.The report adds that the legal process continued for decades and in 2015, a court placed the property under receivership, but the case remained active as attorneys representing Hoffman sought additional time and the county granted extensions.Recognition complicates the pictureWhile the county pursued enforcement, the unusual compound developed a following among architects, neighbors, environmentalists and others fascinated by its unconventional design. As per SFGATE, Marin County's Architectural Commission recognized the property's architectural significance in 2016. A year later, a petition supporting Hoffman attracted 7,132 signatures. The property's historic status received an additional boost in 2024, when The Last Resort was added to the National Register of Historic Places. The designation, however, did not resolve the underlying dispute over its unpermitted construction.Hoffman has acknowledged that the buildings lacked proper permits but has maintained that they were not unsafe. Enforcement actions and fines did little to prevent continued activity at the property, adds the report.Ordered to leaveThe long-running case reached a decisive point when Marin County Superior Court ordered Hoffman to vacate the compound. A court-appointed receiver took control of the property on Sept. 15, according to the county. And now, it remains unclear when the property will be put up for sale. Hoffman is temporarily staying with friends as he considers what comes next. Friends helped remove the tea and some artwork from the compound, but much of his property remains behind. Hoffman estimated that as much as 50,000 pounds of tea had been stored inside the hand-built caves, informs the online report.An uncertain futureThe legal battle has also come at considerable personal cost. Hoffman estimates he has spent about $1 million on attorney fees over the years. His current attorney is continuing to represent him without payment. For now, the future of The Last Resort remains uncertain.
Article Summary: David Lee Hoffman, 82, moved onto the Marin County property more than 53 years ago. Beginning in the 1970s and 1980s, he constructed structures that supported his approach to sustainable living and provided storage for his tea business and other belongings. The compound eventually grew to at least 36 structures, many of them built without the permits required by the county.

Article Title: A California retiree began picking up litter alone on daily walks in 2020; six years later, her volunteer group has removed about 750,000 pounds of trash and now organises valley-wide cleanups
Article Text: Life always has a purpose, and the fun part is that you get to decide it. You can spend a fine morning sleeping through it or volunteering your time for a purpose. For Jill Mather her retirement wasn't going as planned. After decades of working 80-hour weeks in the restaurant business, she had dreamt of travelling, relaxing and spending time with old friends. But soon, COVID-19 struck and Jill was itching to do something.“I can take a long walk at least,” she told herself one morning, and headed out to stroll 4 miles through her San Fernando neighbourhood. She did it again the next day, but as she walked block after block, she noticed there was litter everywhere — cans, bottles and trash. The next morning she grabbed numerous plastic grocery bags and headed out on her walk with a renewed purpose. “That’s a great idea,” neighbours called out when they spotted Jill picking up trash. After a few days, she wondered, Would others like to walk with me?Excited, she posted on the Nextdoor app: 'I walk every morning and pick up trash. If you want to join, meet me in front of the coffee shop at 8 AM'. The next day, she was stunned to see a dozen people show up.She handed out bags and together, they cleaned up a nearby park.When they were all done, they went for a coffee. "When can we do this again?" everyone asked. Soon, every morning, Jill and a rotating crew gathered for two hours of walking and cleaning. She named her group Volunteers Cleaning Communities. They turned in recyclables found on streets, parks and a stretch of State Route 118 and used the cash to buy heavy-duty bags, vests and backpacks.After COVID restrictions lifted, more than 100 people began showing up at least once a week. To keep things interesting, Jill also organised a game night every third month and a monthly birthday celebration. VCC members have formed close friendships. One couple even met, fell in love and got married.“They are my new family,” says Emilie Koster, a former UCLA volunteer. “When COVID struck, we volunteers were the first to be sent home. Then I heard about VCC. It’s easier to do something meaningful when you’re with like-minded people.” Over the past six years, VCC members have removed and disposed of nearly three-quarters of a million pounds of trash. “And that doesn’t include the larger items we set out for the city,” Jill said to Woman's World. “We get exercise, improve the community and make friends. It’s a win all around.”
Article Summary: Jill Mather started Volunteers Cleaning Communities after COVID-19 struck. She and a rotating crew gathered for two hours of walking and cleaning. Over the past six years, VCC members have removed and disposed of nearly three-quarters of a million pounds of trash.

Article Title: In 2017, Dubuque turned recycled plastic equal to about 67,000 water bottles into 14 floating islands; the 2,674-sq-ft system now adds plant, fish and bird habitat to Bee Branch Creek
Article Text:
There are 14 islands totaling 2,674 square feet. Each island is a miniature replica of the natural archipelagos of the Mississippi River. Before the islands were placed in the creek, four prototype designs in a variety of shapes and sizes were developed.

Making a buried creek into an asset

A floating home built from recycled plastic

More than just floating gardens

Keeping the islands in good health

Sometimes the answer for a city that has fought floodwaters for years isn’t more concrete, bigger pipes or taller walls. In Dubuque, Iowa, an old creek that was reopened became the site of an unusual experiment: 14 floating islands made partly from thousands of recycled plastic bottles. The islands were installed in 2017 as part of the Bee Branch Creek restoration and were designed to do more than just add greenery. Today, they help protect the creek, improve water quality and provide small pockets of habitat for fish, birds and aquatic life, states an online report by IECA News. Scroll down to read the details.Flooding has been a problem in Dubuque for a long time, especially in the 7-square-mile Bee Branch Watershed, where more than half of the city's residents live or work. Repeated flash floods damaged some 1,300 homes and businesses, with widespread destruction to buildings, roads and stormwater infrastructure, adds the report.The city responded by daylighting the Bee Branch, a creek that had been buried in a storm sewer about a century ago. The waterway's reintroduction into the landscape allowed natural features to be incorporated into the flood mitigation project.There are 14 islands totaling 2,674 square feet. Each island is a miniature replica of the natural archipelagos of the Mississippi River.Before the islands were placed in the creek, four prototype designs in a variety of shapes and sizes were developed, states IECA News. They constructed their primary floating structures from some 67,000 recycled BPA-free water bottles. Also, native plants were added along with carefully selected pieces of driftwood to create year-round useful habitat. And, fencing around the islands protects the new vegetation from waterfowl. Stainless-steel cables anchor the structures to the creek bed and the flexible anchoring permits the islands to shift with changing water levels and flow directions. The project was partially funded by grants and donations and cost $176,000, states the report.The islands perform a variety of ecological functions. Their construction is such that their structures interrupt the wave energy and this helps to reduce erosion along the edges of the creek. They also serve as barriers to slow water as it moves around the islands, allowing suspended sediment to settle and helping keep the water clear. Now, plants absorb nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, on the islands. Preventing these nutrients from entering waterways can help reduce the amount of nutrients that eventually contribute to ecological problems downstream in the Mississippi River and Gulf of Mexico. Below the surface, the islands can be even more valuable. The plant roots and the floating structures provide space for biofilms, microorganisms that can help break down pollutants. The roots below the water also provide shelter to fish and juvenile aquatic species, and insects and crustaceans use the vegetation as part of the wider food web. And birds also use the islands as resting places and potential nesting habitat above the water.As per the report, the project also shows that nature-based infrastructure needs ongoing maintenance. The islands are regularly checked for buoyancy, vegetation and anchoring systems. A 2019 inspection found most plants were thriving, but some had to be replaced after animal interference and parts of protective fencing needed repairs. Dubuque’s experience shows that careful site selection, native vegetation, durable materials, secure anchoring and regular maintenance are important factors for other communities considering similar projects. What started out as a piece of a flood-control project has turned into something bigger: a working part of urban ecology. On Bee Branch Creek, recycled plastic is now the foundation of living habitat, and the floating islands show how flood infrastructure can create room for nature, as well.Images Courtesy: IECA News and istock
Article Summary: Dubuque, Iowa, installed 14 floating islands in Bee Branch Creek as part of a flood mitigation project. Each island is a miniature replica of the natural archipelagos of the Mississippi River. Plant roots and the floating structures provide space for biofilms, microorganisms that can help break down pollutants. Stainless-steel cables anchor the structures to the creek bed.

Article Title: An Ohio farmer watched gullies repeatedly cut through his family's 700-acre farm and decided to change how he worked the land; decades later, the family operation has grown to 8,000 acres while becomi
Article Text:
The Kellogg story is also one of persistence. He began farming at 14 after his father left agriculture to care for his ill wife. By his senior year of high school, Bill was managing 700 acres, much of it through relationships with older farmers in the community.

From erosion control to precision farming

Adapting instead of following a formula

A farm built through difficult times

Conservation as a family legacy

For Bill Kellogg, conservation did not begin with a government program, a sustainability label or a push for recognition. It began with gullies. Watching water repeatedly carve through his family’s rolling farmland convinced him that the way the ground was being worked had to change. What followed was a decades-long effort to protect the soil while building a larger, more efficient and profitable farm. Scroll down to read the details.According to a report by Farm Progress, Kellogg’s original 700-acre operation has expanded to about 8,000 acres, with 1,800 acres owned and the remainder rented. Along the way, conservation evolved from grass waterways and water and sediment control basins into a much broader system. Today, the Hardin County farm uses grid soil testing, no-till and strip-till practices, precision nutrient management, cover crops, buffer strips, subsurface drainage, pollinator habitat and about 60 acres of waterways.The shift toward precision agriculture accelerated when Bill’s son, Shane, became involved in the operation. Grid soil sampling began in 1999, giving the family a clearer picture of how nutrients were moving through their fields and how the soil responded to management decisions.Strip-till eventually became a particularly visible part of the farm’s approach. Instead of broadcasting fertilizer across an entire field, the Kelloggs began banding nutrients where crops could access them more efficiently. The approach has helped reduce fertilizer use while maintaining or improving yields, states the online report.The Kelloggs do not treat conservation as a one-size-fits-all system. Cover crops, for example, are used selectively, particularly on rolling ground where they can provide greater erosion protection. The farm also is not strictly no-till. Tillage generally remains shallow, rarely going beyond two inches except when drainage or leveling work requires deeper disturbance, and that flexibility extends to fertilizer decisions. With phosphate prices expected to rise above $900 per ton, the family is reconsidering chicken litter as a nutrient source, adds the Farm Progress report. The farm used the material 15 to 20 years ago and is now examining whether bringing it back could make economic sense.The Kellogg story is also one of persistence. He began farming at 14 after his father left agriculture to care for his ill wife. By his senior year of high school, Bill was managing 700 acres, much of it through relationships with older farmers in the community. The farm survived the severe agricultural crisis of the early 1980s, when Bill faced foreclosure and sold possessions to keep the operation afloat. A combination of family help and a shrewd investment in payment-in-kind certificates helped him emerge from the debt crisis, states the report. Those experiences shaped a straightforward financial philosophy: profitability matters alongside stewardship. And that principle remains central as Shane manages the farm’s day-to-day operations and works to expand what his father built.The Kelloggs’ conservation work gained a wider audience after they joined a Farm Bureau and Natural Resources Conservation Service demonstration project following the 2014 Toledo water crisis. The family later became involved with H2Ohio and has opened its farm to thousands of visitors, including students, officials and journalists.Their efforts recently earned the family the Ohio Conservation Farm Family Award. The farm now involves multiple generations, with Bill, Shane, Jacinta Burd and their families contributing to its future.Images Courtesy: Farm Progress
Article Summary: Bill Kellogg began farming at 14 after his father left agriculture to care for his ill wife. Kellogg’s original 700-acre operation has expanded to about 8,000 acres. Grid soil sampling began in 1999, giving the family a clearer picture of how nutrients were moving through their fields.

Article Title: US extends visa curbs on Palestine officials, blocks President Abbas from UN General Assembly
Article Text:
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas appears on a screen as he addresses the 80th United Nations General Assembly (UNGA)

The United States has extended visa restrictions on Palestinian Authority officials and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization, preventing President Mahmoud Abbas and other Palestinian officials from travelling to the US ahead of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.According to Reuters, the US state department said it had determined that the Palestinian Authority and PLO continued to engage in actions that Washington considers inconsistent with commitments made under US laws. The restrictions come ahead of the annual UN gathering, where Palestinian statehood and the Israel-Palestinian conflict are expected to remain major issues.The state department said the Palestinian leadership had continued to pursue measures against Israel through international bodies, including the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice. Washington also cited efforts to secure international recognition of a Palestinian state outside negotiations with Israel.The US has previously said such actions violate commitments made by the Palestinian Authority and PLO under the PLO Commitments Compliance Act of 1989 and the Middle East Peace Commitments Act of 2002. The administration also cited what it described as payments to individuals involved in terrorism and the glorification of terrorism.The restrictions are tied to two US laws governing Palestinian commitments. The PLO Commitments Compliance Act of 1989 requires Washington to assess whether the PLO is meeting commitments on recognising Israel, accepting UN resolutions and renouncing violence.The Middle East Peace Commitments Act of 2002 similarly requires the US to assess compliance by the PLO and Palestinian Authority with commitments made during the Oslo peace process, including resolving outstanding issues through negotiations and peaceful means.The restrictions will prevent Abbas and other affected Palestinian officials from travelling to New York for the UN General Assembly. The US imposed similar visa restrictions last year, and the latest decision extends those measures ahead of this year’s UN session.The state department said the restrictions do not apply to Palestinian officials covered by a waiver for the Palestinian Mission to the UN. The waiver allows accredited Palestinian diplomats to enter the US and participate in UN-related activities despite the broader visa restrictions.The US decision comes as the Palestinian leadership faces growing diplomatic pressure over its international campaign for recognition of statehood and legal action against Israel. Washington has repeatedly opposed efforts to pursue Palestinian statehood through international forums rather than through direct negotiations with Israel.
Article Summary: US state department said it had determined that the Palestinian Authority and PLO continued to engage in actions that Washington considers inconsistent with commitments made under US laws. The restrictions come ahead of the annual UN gathering, where Palestinian statehood and the Israel-Palestinian conflict are expected to remain major issues.

Article Title: Australia to bar foreign students from bringing families, target 225,000 net migration by 2028
Article Text:
Australia home affairs minister Tony Burke is expected to announce the changes.

New restrictions on student families

Migration becomes a political issue

Student numbers and pressure on housing

Australia is preparing to stop international students from bringing their partners and children with them while they study, as the government moves to reduce migration and tighten rules for temporary visa holders, media reports said on Thursday.Home affairs minister Tony Burke is expected to announce the changes in a speech at the National Press Club later in the day. The government plans to bring net overseas migration down to 225,000 by 2028, compared with about 300,000 currently, public broadcaster ABC News reported. Burke's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Under the current system, international students can bring dependent children under 18 to Australia. Their spouses or partners are also allowed to work, although the number of hours they can work depends on the student's course.The proposed changes would remove the option for students to bring their families while they study. The government is also expected to tighten rules governing temporary migrants who want to switch to another visa.The announcement comes as the hard-right One Nation party gains support in recent polls and pushes for a much larger reduction in temporary migration.The party said this week that it wanted to cut the number of temporary migrants by 750,000 over three years, giving Australians "breathing space".One Nation describes its approach as "Australia first" and has proposed reducing net overseas migration to 130,000 after the initial three-year period. It says the programme would be reviewed every year.Australia's migration intake rose sharply after the country reopened its borders in February 2022, following nearly two years of Covid restrictions. International students, backpackers and temporary skilled workers contributed to the increase.Migration has since declined over the past two years, but critics continue to argue that high numbers of newcomers are putting pressure on housing and infrastructure and affecting social cohesion.Official figures show net overseas migration reached 306,000 in the year to June 30, 2025. International students accounted for more than half of that total. Net migration stood at 429,000 in 2024, after reaching a record 518,000 in 2023.The proposed restrictions would affect international students and other temporary migrants, as the government seeks to reduce the overall number of people entering and remaining in Australia.
Article Summary: Government plans to bring net overseas migration down to 225,000 by 2028. Under current system, international students can bring dependent children under 18 to Australia. Their spouses or partners are also allowed to work, although the number of hours they can work depends on the student's course.

Article Title: 'A bit chubby': Memoir claims King Charles fat-shamed Diana; was 'giddily elated' by her death
Article Text:
File photo: Princess Diana and then-Prince Charles at their wedding

‘Like a lottery winner’ after Diana’s death

Charles fat-shames Diana

‘We’ll forget her soon enough’

Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, is set to release a memoir that makes a series of deeply personal claims about his sister’s relationship with King Charles, alleging that the then-Prince Charles sounded “giddily elated — like a lottery winner” when he called after Diana’s death in 1997 and that he once told her, shortly after their engagement, “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”The allegations appear in Spencer’s forthcoming memoir titled ‘Swan Song: Diana, My Sister’, which is being serialised ahead of its publication. The book draws on Spencer’s recollections of his sister’s life, marriage and death nearly three decades ago.Buckingham Palace has already issued an unusually strong response to the book’s claims. While saying it does not comment on books as a matter of principle, a Palace spokesperson said King Charles was mindful that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory” even many years after a loss.Spencer writes that he was at his home in Cape Town with his children when he learnt that Diana had been killed in a car crash in Paris on August 31, 1997.After a series of calls confirming her death, Charles called Spencer, according to the memoir.Spencer claims that while other callers were stunned and struggled to express their condolences, Charles “sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner”.He says Charles told him he had informed William and Harry of their mother’s death in their bedrooms at Balmoral.Spencer describes the conversation as “strangely matter-of-fact” given the circumstances.Looking back, Spencer says he suspects Charles may have been thinking about how Diana’s death could free him to marry the woman he loved, an interpretation that forms part of Spencer’s own recollection of the conversation.Another claim concerns Diana’s weight and eating disorder in the months before her wedding.Spencer writes that Diana was already struggling with an eating disorder when Charles allegedly squeezed her waist shortly after their engagement and remarked: “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”He says the comment devastated Diana. According to Spencer, she later told him that her waist shrank from 29 inches to 23½ inches between her engagement and wedding.Spencer also claims that Diana had told a friend that Charles had confided to her on the eve of their wedding that he was happy to marry her but was not actually in love with her.Spencer recounts another alleged conversation with Charles during preparations for Diana’s funeral.He says he objected to William and Harry walking behind their mother’s coffin and subsequently received a call from Charles. Spencer describes Charles as becoming angry during the exchange.He claims that Charles eventually told him: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough!”Spencer writes that he was so shocked by the remark that he told Charles he could not believe he had said it before ending the call.The Palace’s response came after this earlier extract was published. It did not directly address the individual allegations but questioned the reliability of memories shaped by grief decades after Diana’s death.The memoir also contains claims about Diana’s funeral arrangements, her decision to divorce Charles, her relationship with the royal household and her experiences during the breakdown of her marriage. Spencer says the book is intended, in part, to challenge what he considers “untruths” that emerged after his sister’s death.
Article Summary: Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, is set to release a memoir that makes a series of deeply personal claims about his sister’s relationship with King Charles. Spencer alleges that the then-Prince Charles sounded “giddily elated — like a lottery winner” when he called after Diana’S death in 1997. He also claims that he once told her, shortly after their engagement, “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”

Article Title: Denver is using heat from sewage beneath the National Western Center to warm and cool seven buildings, now covering about 90% of their heating and cooling needs
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing heat-recovery equipment that transfers thermal energy from wastewater to a separate building-energy system at Denver’s National Western Center. Credits - Google Gemini

Getting heat from an unexpected source

AI-generated representative image showing district-energy infrastructure serving buildings at Denver’s National Western Center. Credits - Google Gemini

A growing system

Most towns treat and dispose of wastewater, but Denver captures the heat before it goes out the door. Engineers created a system beneath the National Western Center, a 250-acre complex in north Denver focused on agriculture, food innovation and western history, that sucks heat directly out of sewage flowing through the city’s pipes and uses it to heat and cool buildings above ground.The system, which came online in April 2022, now meets about 90 per cent of the heating and cooling needs of multiple campus buildings, including the Vida and Terra buildings at the Colorado State University Spur campus and a nearby event centre. The plant, anchored by two SHARC 880 units from equipment manufacturer SHARC Energy, processes over 3,000 gallons of untreated wastewater per minute as part of a 3.8 megawatt district energy network and is the largest sewer heat recovery system in North America, according to SHARC Energy.The idea behind the technology is simple, but the engineering can be complicated. The wastewater from houses and businesses is usually at a rather constant temperature throughout the year, roughly in the mid-fifties to mid-seventies degrees Fahrenheit, independent of the weather outside. In winter, a heat exchanger extracts heat from the wastewater and transfers it to a separate loop of clean water that is supplied for heating to surrounding buildings.In summer, the same system runs backward, drawing heat out of the buildings and instead rejecting it into the wastewater. It’s a way of employing the sewage as a cooling source.That separation between the wastewater and the clean water loop keeps the two systems fully isolated, with no contamination risk to the buildings served. An article describing the project’s development, which appeared in Colorado State University System , details how the 18-month design and construction effort relied on a consortium led by CenTrio, the district energy firm that runs day-to-day operations at the facility.Moving the project from concept to execution involved rerouting a large piece of city infrastructure. Denver-based Saunders collaborated with engineering firm AECOM. Instead of individual boilers and chillers for each building, the system extracts thermal energy from a sewer pipeline nearby and distributes that energy through a closed-loop network. This approach, known as district energy, is typically more efficient and cheaper to maintain over the life of the system than individual building systems.There is a strong environmental rationale for the system. When the first phases of the National Western Center are fully built out, the heat recovery plant is expected to prevent around 2,600 metric tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions each year, which is roughly equivalent to removing about 6.5 million miles of vehicle travel from Denver’s roads each year. The system already serves seven buildings, with more than one million square feet of space, and its designers built in capacity for further expansion when more parts of the campus come online in future construction phases.For a city looking to reduce its dependence on natural gas, extracting heat from something as unglamorous as sewage offers a realistic solution to an age-old problem, taking energy that would otherwise be flushed down the drain and putting it to use warming the buildings above it instead.
Article Summary: Engineers created a system beneath the National Western Center, a 250-acre complex in north Denver. It sucks heat directly out of sewage flowing through the city’s pipes and uses it to heat and cool buildings above ground. The system, which came online in April 2022, now meets about 90 per cent of the heating and cooling needs of multiple campus buildings.

Article Title: In 2007, a California engineer set out by bicycle and rowboat to circle Earth alone; five years later, he returned after 41,196 miles and three ocean crossings powered only by himself
Article Text:
AI representation: California engineer left by bicycle and rowboat to circle Earth alone. Image credits: Chatgpt

The route: Bodega Bay to Bodega Bay, 10 July 2007 to 21 July 2012

49 transatlantic rowers and a 10% loss of body mass

Maximal sustainable energy intake during transatlantic ocean rowing is insufficient for total energy expenditure and skeletal muscle mass maintenance

View from Mount Townsend towards Mount Kosciuszko. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A 37-year-old's 38-day solo row across the North Atlantic in 2018

The Physical and Psychological Experience of Rowing the North Atlantic Solo and Unassisted

On 10 July 2007, Seattle-based engineer Erden Eruç set out from a pier in Bodega Bay, California, to complete the first solo circumnavigation of the globe using human power, a journey that, according to Guinness World Records , involved rowing, kayaking, hiking, and cycling. Post Alley reports that he cashed out his 401(k) to fund the expedition, while Back in America describes the boat in detail.Erden Eruç arrived back at the same pier in Bodega Bay, California, on 21 July 2012, completing what Guinness World Records recognizes as the first solo circumnavigation of the globe using human power. Guinness World Records puts the journey at 5 years, 11 days, 12 hours, and 22 minutes, covering a total distance of 66,299 km (41,196 miles). He is recorded as the first person to complete a solo human-powered circumnavigation, and he was also the first to row across the three oceans: the Pacific Ocean, the Indian Ocean , and the Atlantic Ocean. Below are the route, followed by two research papers that offer context on what ocean rowing demands of the body.Post Alley traces Eruç's route up to about the halfway point of the expedition. He rowed from California to Australia, where he cycled across the country and climbed Mount Kosciuszko, the highest peak on the continent. From there, he rowed across the Indian Ocean to Tanzania and climbed Kilimanjaro. After this, he cycled to Namibia. Guinness World Records covers the Atlantic leg.Eruç rowed from Lüderitz, Namibia, to Güiria, Venezuela, and then cycled to Carúpano, Venezuela. He next crossed the Gulf of Mexico to Cameron, Louisiana, USA, arriving on 27 May 2012. Finally, he cycled to reach Bodega Bay.Eruç used a rowing boat on the ocean, a bicycle on land, and kayaks along the coastlines. The initial circumnavigation by Eruç took about five years, with lengthy stops in between for repairs and planning the next step in the journey. Although the total duration is well documented, there is no exact, reliable figure for how many of those days were spent traveling and how many were spent resting.No study has followed Eruç himself, but research on transatlantic rowers suggests what a single ocean crossing can demand of the body. The paperappeared in Experimental Physiology in November 2023. The Experimental Physiology paper reports data from 49 rowers (32 males and 17 females, ages 24-67 years) who took part in the Talisker Whisky Atlantic Challenge, with complete datasets from 25 rowers in 2020 and 24 in 2021. According to the paper, the rowers worked in a continuous pattern of two- to three-hour shifts, 24 hours a day, for a minimum of 12 hours of rowing daily. The race covers roughly 3,000 miles, and typical race durations in the paper range from about 40 to 59 days, with the rowers in this study averaging 46 days at sea.Energy expenditure was determined using the doubly labeled water technique during the last week of participation in the challenge. Energy expenditure was 2.5-fold higher than the resting metabolic rate in males and 2.3-fold in females; energy intake was equal for both groups. Nevertheless, there was a significant reduction in body mass in both groups, by 10.2% in males and 10.0% in females. Thus, the scientists conclude that sustainable energy intake in a rower is less than the energy expenditure and energy needs of the skeletal muscles.The paperwas published in Wilderness and Environmental Medicine in 2020. It followed one 37-year-old man who left St. John's, Newfoundland, on 27 June 2018. He traveled roughly 2,000 miles (3,218 km) over 38 days, 6 hours and 49 minutes before arriving at the Isles of Scilly. He scored each day regarding his effort, physical feelings, and mood. Daily ratings of perceived effort, body sensations, and mood were collected during the crossing to assess its progress, transforming one athlete's experience into an insight into the physical and psychological difficulties of unsupported ocean crossing. The research being a case study, the results obtained can only serve as an illustration and not be generalized, but nevertheless provide a unique daily account of how difficult the crossing really was.A hurricane named Chris prevented him from rowing for 8 days, and a normal rowing day saw him rowing for 10 to 11 hours. His ratings for pain, loneliness, boredom, anxiety, and frustration remained low on average, while fatigue, restfulness, positive affect, calmness, and confidence were moderate. The study adds that only 16 people had completed the transatlantic row, while 31 attempts had failed, three of them ending with the rowers lost at sea. Because the study features a single rower, it cannot stand in as a profile of Eruç; it serves only as context for what a long solo ocean crossing can involve. However, Guinness World Records shows his row between Lüderitz and Guiria from 10 October 2011 to 11 March 2012 as the record for the longest nonstop distance rowed across the Atlantic at 5,788 miles. This is almost twice the distance of the transatlantic row in the above mentioned Experimental Physiology study, and over 3 times the time spent at sea.
Article Summary: Seattle-based engineer Erden Eruç set out from a pier in Bodega Bay, California, to complete the first solo circumnavigation of the globe using human power. He rowed from California to Australia, where he cycled across the country and climbed Mount Kosciuszko, the highest peak on the continent. From there, he rowed across. the Indian Ocean to Tanzania and climbed Kilimanjaro. After this, hecycled to Namibia. and then cycled to Carúpano, Venezuela. He next crossed the Gulf of Mexico to Cameron, Louisiana,

Article Title: 'What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable': Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row on stage
Article Text:
Ed Sheeran takes stage to address Macklemore row.

'What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic'

Why was Macklemore removed?

Gaza death toll

Ed Sheeran on Saturday addressed the controversy surrounding rapper Macklemore's removal from his US tour, saying he could no longer “hide” how he feels about the Israel-Palestine conflict.The controversy began after Macklemore made pro-Palestinian remarks during Sheeran’s September 4 and 5 shows at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, including saying “Free Palestine” and performing his protest song “Hind’s Hall”.Speaking at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field, Sheeran opened his solo concert by addressing the controversy and the wider debate over free speech that has engulfed his Loop Tour.Sheeran said he wanted his music and concerts to focus on unity and humanity rather than politics. However, he said the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel were horrific, while describing the situation in Gaza as “catastrophic and unjustifiable.”“I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” Sheeran said.He acknowledged that he had made “mistakes” while navigating the difficult decisions surrounding the controversy.“My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone,” he said, adding that he remained committed to his fans, according to BBC.“Now, I want to address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand,” he said.“I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics. But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore," he added.Sheeran further described the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel as “horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain”.“What happened in Israel and at the Nome Museum Festival on October 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain,” Sheeran said.“What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of of devastation and loss of civilian lives, of children's lives, and this systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked,” he added.Sheeran said he was trying “to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times and listening and learning, because I do not know enough”.He also said he was “deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performance”. The singer ended his remarks by saying he wanted his concerts to remain spaces where people with opposing views could come together.“I am honestly so grateful that you're here tonight with me,” he told the audience. “This concert is still a place where everyone is welcome and everyone here can stand beside people that have opposing views,” he added.Macklemore was subsequently removed from the remaining US dates after venues objected to his participation, according to the tour promoter. Several supporting acts later withdrew from the tour in solidarity.Macklemore’s remarks drew criticism from some Jewish and pro-Israel organisations, with the Israeli-American Council calling for him to be removed from the tour.Messina Touring Group, the promoter behind the US leg of Sheeran’s Loop Tour, later announced that Macklemore would no longer perform on the remaining dates.The promoter said venues had informed it that they would not allow concerts featuring the rapper to proceed, potentially leading to cancellations affecting hundreds of thousands of ticket holders.Sheeran has said the decision was made by the promoter and venues, not by him. He also expressed concern about venues deciding in advance what performers can say on stage.Macklemore has said the decision came after pressure from venue owners, including Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran was scheduled to perform.Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the rapper of hate speech and said he was “only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas”.The controversy intensified after several artists withdrew from Sheeran’s tour in solidarity with Macklemore. Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, Danish band Lukas Graham and members of Sheeran’s touring band Beoga were among those who pulled out.Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, also withdrew from the South American leg of the tour. The artists cited concerns about freedom of speech and the decision to remove Macklemore.Macklemore later said he and Sheeran had held “difficult conversations” following the MetLife shows. He maintained his support for Palestinians and said he did not regret using the tour stage to speak about the conflict.Macklemore said Wednesday that he would donate $1 million to Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the contribution.Despite the controversy, several fans attending Sheeran’s Philadelphia concert said they continued to support the singer. Some said they had hesitated about attending because of the dispute but ultimately chose to go ahead with the show.Others attended a protest outside the stadium instead, while some fans said they wanted to put the controversy aside and enjoy the music. Reuters reported that fans at the concert largely expressed support for Sheeran despite the backlash.Pro-Palestinian protesters also gathered outside Lincoln Financial Field ahead of the concert, criticising Macklemore’s removal from the tour. Sheeran’s Loop Tour is scheduled to continue with shows across North and South America.Israeli airstrikes killed at least three Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on Saturday, according to health officials. One strike near the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza killed Basir Al-Bursh, the son of Munir Al-Bursh, director-general of Gaza’s health ministry, medics and family members said.Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, which began after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.A US-brokered ceasefire agreed last year calls for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made as negotiators remain divided over Hamas disarming and Israel withdrawing its troops.More than 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect, according to territory health officials. The Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed during the same period.
Article Summary: Ed Sheeran addressed the controversy surrounding rapper Macklemore's removal from his US tour. He said he could no longer “hide” how he feels about the Israel-Palestine conflict. The singer said he wanted his music and concerts to focus on unity and humanity rather than politics.

Article Title: Something big brewing? Trump abruptly leaves Camp David, returns to White House
Article Text:
West Asia tensions soar; Trump cuts short Camp David stay

US President Donald Trump cut short his weekend stay at Camp David and returned to the White House on Saturday, a day earlier than scheduled, as tensions escalated across West Asia.The administration did not explain why Trump was returning a day earlier from Camp David, a secluded presidential retreat in rural Maryland, as previously announced.The move came as the US state department and several American diplomatic missions across West Asia issued security alerts, warning of the “potential for unforeseen escalation” in the region.“This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly,” the State department warning said, urging Americans to reconsider travel to and through the region.The latest US warnings followed a reported escalation involving Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. Saudi Arabia said the group launched a ballistic missile towards Riyadh early Saturday, while the Houthis said they had targeted “sensitive sites”, adding to concerns that the wider conflict could spread further across the region.Against this backdrop, Iran conveyed seven conditions to Washington for restarting negotiations to end the conflict. Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera that Qatar had passed the conditions to Washington and that Tehran was awaiting Trump’s response.Rezaei publicly outlined three of the demands: an end to the war on all fronts, the release of Iran’s frozen funds and an end to the US naval blockade. He did not publicly detail the remaining four conditions.Rezaei also warned that Iran was prepared for a “decisive war” if Washington rejected its demands, saying Trump’s threats would not achieve results. He said Tehran remained in contact with Qatar as a mediator and was awaiting a response from the US.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump cuts short his weekend stay at Camp David and returns to the White House. The move came as the US state department and several American diplomatic missions across West Asia issued security alerts. The latest US warnings followed a reported escalation involving Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.

Article Title: 'Sad chapter': Trump slams US Supreme Court over tariff, birthright citizenship rulings
Article Text: US President Donald Trump on Saturday criticised the United States Supreme Court over its rulings on tariffs and birthright citizenship, accusing the top court of lacking the courage to “make America great again”.In a post on Truth Social, Trump described the court's decisions as “faulty, political and ridiculous”, claiming they had cost the country trillions of dollars and “forever damaged” the process through which people become US citizens.“Unfortunately, the United States Supreme Court has lacked the courage to make America great again,” Trump said.“Over the last 6 months, with their faulty, political, and ridiculous decisions on tariffs and birthright citizenship, they have cost the United States of America trillions of Dollars, and forever damaged the way people become citizens of our great Country. It has been a sad chapter in the life and times of America, but we will prevail!” he added.Trump's remarks come amid a series of legal battles between his administration and the Supreme Court over his tariff policies and efforts to restrict birthright citizenship.In February, the Supreme Court struck down most of Trump's sweeping tariff measures, ruling that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorise the president to impose the extensive import duties.The ruling triggered a major refund process for importers that had paid the disputed tariffs. According to a US Customs and Border Protection court filing, around USD 100 billion in refunds had been completed and sent to the US Treasury for disbursement by July 31. About USD 128.68 billion in potential and certified refunds had been accepted for processing.The tariff ruling also created financial and administrative challenges for the US government, with customs authorities developing a new system to calculate and process refunds for affected importers.Trump has continued to defend his tariff strategy, arguing that the measures are aimed at protecting American industries, boosting domestic manufacturing and addressing trade imbalances.His administration has also faced legal challenges over its attempt to restrict birthright citizenship. The administration has argued that existing interpretations of the 14th Amendment permit citizenship restrictions in certain circumstances, while opponents have challenged the policy in court.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has criticised the Supreme Court over its rulings on tariffs and birthright citizenship. Trump described the court's decisions as “faulty, political and ridiculous” He claimed they had cost the country trillions of dollars and “forever damaged” the process through which people become US citizens.

Article Title: In 1952, Rachel Carson bought a Maine cottage and studied tidal pools; six years later she began writing Silent Spring
Article Text:
Image: Left/Exterior of the Rachel Carson House/NPS/Right/Carson in 1943/ National Digital Library of the United States Fish and Wildlife Service

Rachel Carson's career before her 1952 Maine cottage

Why Rachel Carson bought a cottage in Maine

Carson and Bob Hines researching off the East Coast in 1952 (Image: National Digital Library of the United States Fish and Wildlife Service)

How Rachel Carson came to begin writing Silent Spring

The impact of Silent Spring and Rachel Carson's lasting legacy

In 1952, American biologist and writer Rachel Carson resigned from her government job and bought a cottage in Southport, Maine, where she began original research on tidal pool ecosystems. Six years later, in 1958, she began work on what would become her most famous book, Silent Spring, published in 1962. The book exposed the dangers of indiscriminate pesticide use and helped spark the modern environmental movement. Here's how Carson's path from marine biologist to bestselling author led to one of the most influential books of the twentieth century.Born in 1907, Carson grew up on a farm in Springdale, Pennsylvania, where her parents encouraged her exploration of the natural world. According to the National Park Service, she studied English at Pennsylvania College for Women before switching to biology in her junior year, graduating with honours in 1929. She went on to earn a Master of Science in zoology and genetics from Johns Hopkins University, then taught there and at the University of Maryland. In 1936, she joined the Bureau of Fisheries, later the Fish and Wildlife Service, writing scientific pamphlets for the public.She published her first book, Under the Sea-Wind, in 1941.By 1949, Carson had become Editor-in-Chief of all Department of publications. In 1951, she completed her second book, The Sea Around Us, which was serialised by The New Yorker and spent months on The New York Times bestseller list. The following year, in 1952, she resigned from her government post and bought a cottage in Southport, Maine, where she conducted original research on tidal pool ecosystems. This research fed into her third book, The Edge of the Sea, written in 1955, which completed her anthology on the natural history of the ocean.In 1956, Carson moved into a new home she had designed in Silver Spring, Maryland, shaping the asymmetrical one-storey brick house around the surrounding natural landscape. Two years later, in 1958, she began work on Silent Spring, which focused on mankind's destruction of nature and the interconnectedness of living things, from pesticides running off into pastures to their eventual presence in human milk supplies. She criticised scientists for endorsing widespread pesticide use, including DDT, despite its harmful effects, while stopping short of calling for pesticides to be abandoned altogether in favour of a more conscientious approach.Published in 1962, Silent Spring provoked an immediate reaction, the chemical industry spent hundreds of thousands of dollars attempting to discredit Carson, while President Kennedy convened the Presidential Science Advisory Committee to examine her claims, which it ultimately verified. The book sold over 600,000 copies that year, and Carson's work is widely credited as a catalyst for the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970. Carson died of cancer in her Silver Spring home on 14 April 1964. Four years later, America marked its first Earth Day, and her former home now houses the Rachel Carson Landmark Alliance.
Article Summary: In 1952, American biologist and writer Rachel Carson bought a cottage in Southport, Maine. Six years later, in 1958, she began work on what would become her most famous book, Silent Spring, published in 1962. The book exposed the dangers of indiscriminate pesticide use and helped spark the modern environmental movement.

Article Title: Can't hastily deport to a third country: What US appeals court ruling says
Article Text:
A US Federals Court has ruled that immigrants facing deportation to third countries must be given sufficient notice before being sent to nations where they have no ties.

What are third-country deportations?

A US federal appeals court has ruled that immigrants facing deportation to countries where they have no ties must receive sufficient notice and a meaningful opportunity to challenge their removal before being sent there. A three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit unanimously struck down a Department of Homeland Security policy that allowed the administration to deport immigrants to so-called third countries with little or no advance notice.The ruling means migrants must be allowed to raise concerns if they fear persecution or other harm in the country to which they are being deported.“An individual's right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination,” Circuit Judge Seth Aframe wrote in the ruling.A third-country deportation involves removing an immigrant to a country that is neither their country of citizenship nor necessarily a country where they have family or other ties.The Trump administration has expanded the practice in recent months after reaching agreements with dozens of countries, including Liberia, Ghana, the Central African Republic and Sierra Leone. About 25,000 people have been deported to third countries during the administration's immigration crackdown.The administration has cited diplomatic assurances from receiving countries that deported immigrants will not be mistreated.But the lawsuit challenging the policy argued that migrants were sometimes given little or no opportunity to object before being put on flights to countries where they could face persecution or other serious harm.The appeals court agreed that prior notice and an opportunity to challenge the destination were required. The Washington Post reported that the court found the government had not adequately shown which countries had provided the diplomatic assurances relied upon by the administration.The case follows reports of immigrants being deported to countries they had never visited. ABC News recently reported on a group of Latin American men sent to the Central African Republic who said they were not told their destination until hours into the flight.The latest ruling does not eliminate the government's ability to deport immigrants to third countries. Instead, it requires the administration to provide the procedural protections migrants need to challenge removal to a particular destination before sending them there.The ruling is the latest development in a broader legal battle over the Trump administration's expanded use of third-country deportations.
Article Summary: A US federal appeals court has ruled that immigrants facing deportation to countries where they have no ties must receive sufficient notice. A three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit unanimously struck down a Department of Homeland Security policy that allowed the administration to deport immigrants to so-called third countries with little or no advance notice.

Article Title: 'People who call me a paperwork American': Indian-origin Trump aide triggers MAGA row, says she faces racist comments daily
Article Text:
Harmeet K Dhillon says she faces racist attacks daily.

What happened with Harmeet K Dhillon?

Then a photo of an Indian dinner plate with beef

US Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet K Dhillon was at the center of a mini-MAGA implosion this weekend as she said she faces racist attacks daily. One side of MAGA asked her to leave the US and got blocked by her, while the other side called her a true American. But all of it started with Dhillon's 'Happy weekend' post and then ended with her photo of a beef dinner.From her personal account, Dhillon made a weekend post but made sure to add some punch as she wrote: "Happy weekend and good Shabbos to all — yes, even the people who call me a “paperwork American,” who post racist nonsense for clicks, who haven’t read enough books, who don’t know history. God loves all of you and it’s not too late to stop being wrong."Conservative commentator and author Megan Basham expressed shock that Dhillon was ever called a 'paperwork American' but Dhillon set the record straight and added: "I get racist comments like this daily and many top social media accounts, including many whose shows I have appeared on dozens of times, are spewing this racist crap, and I’m sick of it." Social media users said this must be a dig at Erike Kirk, Sara Gonzales and the MAGA podcasters Dhillon has spoken to."Looks like the Sikh Truck Driver getting stabbed and the Department of Homeland Security posting that image of a Sikh finally made @HarmeetKDhillon reach her breaking point. She just called out Erika Kirk, Sara Gonzalez and the entire MAGA Alternative Media here," one wrote.As Megan Basham defended Dhillon, Megan's old social media posts calling all non-Christians 'demon-worshippers' surfaced and X users asked Basham whether she considered Dhillon too a 'demon worshipper'As Dhillon announced in her weekend wishing post that she was going to spend time with her family, she posted a photo of her Indian dinner plate and detailed the items, including beef. Social media users called her out for eating beef and she said eating beef is not prohibited in the Sikh religion.Dhillon, who was born in Chandigarh, India, moved with her family to the United States after living in London. She attended Dartmouth College before earning her law degree from the University of Virginia. She was nominated by President Donald Trump in December 2024, confirmed by the Senate on April 3, 2025, and sworn in as assistant attorney general for civil rights on April 7, 2025.
Article Summary: US Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet K Dhillon was at the center of a mini-MAGA implosion this weekend as she said she faces racist attacks daily. One side of MAGA asked her to leave the US and got blocked by her, while the other side called her a true American.

Article Title: 'Negotiate or face decisive war': Iran conveys terms to US for restarting talks, sets 7 conditions
Article Text:
Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei laid out the conditions that Iran sent to the US

Iran has formally conveyed its conditions to United States for ending the war, with its top official saying it has set out seven conditions for restarting negotiations while warning that it is also prepared for a “decisive war”.Iran’s supreme national security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview that Qatar had passed Tehran’s conditions to Washington and that Iran was awaiting US President Donald Trump’s response. “Our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade,” Rezaei said.“It is in Washington’s interest to accept these conditions. Trump’s threats will not achieve any results. We are prepared for a decisive war,” he added.In a separate post on X, he confirmed that it had announced seven conditions for starting negotiations with the US, saying Washington would have to accept Iran’s “rights and conditions” if it wanted to “escape the quagmire” and avoid becoming further entangled in the conflict.“It is in Washington’s interest to accept these conditions.Trump’s threats will not achieve any results. We are prepared for a decisive war,” Rezaei added.Meanwhile, Rezaei also told Al Jazeera that Iran was also preparing for the possibility of another US strike, describing it as “very much on the cards”. He said Tehran had changed its military planning and was now focused on US naval assets across the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.He claimed Iran had recently test-fired a multi-warhead anti-ship missile near a US vessel or aircraft carrier and warned that any future Iranian response would include US bases and American commercial interests in the region.At the same time, Rezaei said Tehran was pursuing diplomacy to bring the conflict to an end “as soon as possible”. Qatar and Pakistan have been involved in efforts to restart negotiations between Washington and Tehran after their earlier memorandum of understanding expired.On the nuclear issue, Rezaei said Iran had not decided to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, although he warned that further sanctions or a referral of its nuclear file to the UN Security Council “may push Tehran into withdrawing”.He also said Tehran remained open to an agreement with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz, saying the two sides had come within “a short step” of reaching a deal before it was shelved.The comments come as Washington weighs its next move in the conflict. Trump told Axios this week that he was facing a “big decision” over whether to resume major military action against Iran. “Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not?” Trump had said, adding, “Anything could happen with me.”
Article Summary: Iran's supreme national security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview that Qatar had passed Tehran’s conditions to Washington. “Our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and anend to the naval blockade,” he said. ‘We are prepared for a decisive war,’ he added.

Article Title: Should Indian students abandon the 'American Dream' amid F-1 visa volatility? 4 things immigration experts suggest
Article Text:
Students planning to study in the US in the next 1-2 years should prepare differently, immigration experts suggest.

Choose degree, not America

Take stock of the financial situation

Expect scrutiny and delay as the norm, not the exception

Explore lower-cost alternatives

International students in the US faced immense volatility this year because of several new rules -- some are being proposed, some are coming into effect.
